reference.source: GeneReviews / Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
clinicalPearls: The syndrome links a spinal cord vascular malformation with a cutaneous vascular lesion, both localised to the same body segment (metamere)
The skin lesion is typically a vascular stain or angioma overlying the trunk or back in the dermatome corresponding to the affected spinal level
Patients commonly present with a progressive myelopathy: limb weakness, sensory disturbance, and bladder or bowel dysfunction, sometimes with acute deterioration
The spinal lesion is usually an arteriovenous malformation or fistula that can compromise the cord through mass effect, venous hypertension, or haemorrhage
The metameric distribution reflects a developmental origin affecting a single embryological segment, and it is generally sporadic rather than inherited
Recognition of a segmental cutaneous vascular lesion in someone with myelopathy should prompt dedicated spinal vascular imaging
Management is by a neurovascular multidisciplinary team, with catheter angiography defining the lesion and endovascular embolisation and/or microsurgery used to protect cord function
reference.pathophysiology: Cobb syndrome is a metameric neurocutaneous vascular disorder in which a vascular malformation of the spinal cord and its coverings coexists with a cutaneous vascular lesion in the matching body segment. The shared segmental distribution is thought to arise from a developmental event affecting cells destined for a single metamere, so that skin, vertebral, meningeal, and cord tissues derived from that segment carry the vascular anomaly. The neurological consequences stem from the spinal arteriovenous malformation, which can injure the cord by direct compression, by diverting blood and raising venous pressure with resulting cord ischaemia, or by haemorrhage. The condition is characteristically sporadic.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated spinal arteriovenous malformation or dural arteriovenous fistula
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the spine with contrast to identify the cord vascular malformation and any cord signal change
Spinal catheter angiography to define the vascular anatomy and feeding vessels
Clinical mapping of the cutaneous vascular lesion to the corresponding dermatome
Neurological examination to localise the spinal level and grade deficit
Dermatological assessment of the cutaneous vascular lesion
MRI of the brain if a more extensive metameric syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Acute or rapidly progressive paraparesis or sensory level suggesting cord compromise or haemorrhage
New bladder or bowel dysfunction indicating significant cord involvement
Sudden severe back pain with neurological signs suggesting spinal haemorrhage
Progressive deterioration despite conservative measures, requiring urgent neurovascular intervention
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the size, location, and haemodynamics of the spinal malformation and on the degree of cord injury at presentation. Timely diagnosis and treatment can stabilise or improve neurological function, whereas late presentation with established cord damage or haemorrhage carries a risk of permanent disability.
pitfalls: Treating a truncal vascular birthmark as purely cosmetic and missing the associated spinal malformation
Attributing progressive myelopathy to more common causes without considering a spinal vascular lesion
Delaying spinal vascular imaging in a patient with segmental cutaneous and neurological findings
Underestimating the risk of haemorrhage and cord ischaemia from an untreated arteriovenous malformation
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Definitive treatment of the spinal arteriovenous malformation or fistula by endovascular embolisation and/or microsurgical resection to decompress and protect the cord
Urgent neurosurgical intervention for cord compression, venous hypertension or haemorrhage causing acute or progressive myelopathy
Symptomatic and rehabilitative care: physiotherapy, spasticity management, and bladder and bowel programmes for neurogenic dysfunction
Dermatological management of the segmental cutaneous vascular lesion (angioma or capillary malformation), with laser therapy if symptomatic or cosmetically troubling
Serial neurological examination and interval spinal MRI to monitor the malformation and detect recurrence or progression
Multidisciplinary care coordinated between interventional neuroradiology, spinal neurosurgery, neurology, dermatology and rehabilitation
Escalate immediately for acute neurological deterioration, which may signal intralesional haemorrhage requiring emergency angiography and intervention
